description:
We are a dedicated multidisciplinary team focused on aerospace innovation, human factors engineering, and psychological resilience in deep space exploration. Our mission is to bridge the critical gap between physiological health and psychological well-being for astronauts on long-duration missions.

summary:
ASTROCAM is a space wellness concept designed to support astronauts experiencing stress, fatigue, and isolation during long missions. We developed a website prototype demonstrating a personalized wellness journey, supported by a visual concept of a wall-mounted camera and connected touchscreen inside a spacecraft.

Users select a crew profile, experience a simulated stress assessment, and choose a companion such as a puppy, kitten, plant, or floating ball. The proposed experience offers supportive conversation, guided breathing, relaxation, and other simple activities.

ASTROCAM addresses the human challenges of space exploration by exploring how accessible, personalized support could fit into astronauts’ daily routines. NASA research on isolation and confinement informed the problem definition.

The current prototype demonstrates the interface and intended experience. Stress readings are simulated, and camera-based analysis, autonomous conversation, and offline processing require further development and validation. ASTROCAM aims to make life far from Earth feel a little more human.
details:
ASTROCAM is a space wellness concept that explores how personalized support could become part of an astronaut’s daily routine inside a spacecraft. It combines a website prototype with a visual concept of a wall-mounted camera and connected touchscreen.

HOW IT WORKS

The demonstration begins with the user selecting a crew profile: Alex, Luna, or Max. It then presents a simulated wellness assessment to illustrate how the system might suggest a supportive break.

The user can choose a digital companion, such as a puppy, kitten, plant, or floating ball. The proposed companion experience includes friendly conversation and encouragement to try activities. Users who prefer activities without a companion can access options such as guided breathing, relaxation, interactive activities, or a calm environment.

In a future version, we propose investigating facial expressions and blinking patterns as possible indicators that could inform optional wellness suggestions. These signals require scientific validation and cannot independently establish a person’s psychological state.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

ASTROCAM aims to make short wellness breaks accessible, engaging, and adaptable to individual preferences. Its intended users are astronauts working in isolated and confined environments during long missions.

The project explores whether personalized companionship and simple activities could encourage users to pause and engage with wellness support. These benefits remain hypotheses. We have not measured reductions in stress, cortisol, oxygen consumption, or improvements in mission performance.

TOOLS AND DEVELOPMENT

We used Replit to develop and host the website prototype. ChatGPT supported ideation, content drafting, and prototype development. AI image generation helped visualize the proposed device and spacecraft experience. ElevenLabs supported the preparation of demonstration media, and PowerPoint was used to present the project.

The camera and touchscreen are proposed hardware components illustrated through concept images. We have not built or tested a physical AstroCam device.

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

ASTROCAM brings a proposed monitoring system together with a personalized companion and optional wellness activities in one cabin-based experience. Users can choose the form of interaction they find comfortable.

We considered privacy, consent, ease of use, individual preferences, and the limitations of interpreting facial behavior. Local processing and offline operation are future development goals, rather than demonstrated capabilities.

NASA RESEARCH AND CURRENT STATUS

NASA publications on isolation, confinement, and behavioral health informed our understanding of the problem. We did not integrate a NASA dataset or train a stress-detection model.

The current prototype demonstrates the interface and intended user journey. Stress readings are simulated, while live sensing, autonomous conversation, and hardware integration require further development. ASTROCAM is not a medical or psychological diagnostic tool.

Our next step is to test usability, including task completion, time needed to start an activity, and perceived helpfulness. Any future sensing capability would require specialist collaboration and validation.
